name: An (the heavens)
symbols: the horned crown (the crown of kingship)

primary_sources.name: Enuma Elish (Babylonian Creation Epic)
primary_sources.date: Old Babylonian version c. 18th c. BCE; standard form c. 1100-1000 BCE

primary_sources.name: etcl.mca.edu — Electronic Text Corpus of cuneiform (transliterations + translations)

description_short: The sky god, the supreme deity of the Sumerian pantheon; 'An' means 'sky/heaven'. In the Akkadian period he is called Anu. Father of Enlil and (in some accounts) Enki.
description_long: 'An' (Sumerian; 'Anu' in Akkadian) is the sky god, the supreme deity of the Sumerian pantheon [S5][S6]. 'An' means 'sky' or 'heaven' — the god is the sky itself, the highest of the three cosmic regions (heaven, earth, underworld) [S5]. In the Sumerian period, An was the head of the pantheon; in the Akkadian and Babylonian periods, his supremacy was increasingly ceded to Enlil (and later Marduk) [S1][S6]. An's symbol is the star (the five-pointed star) and his animal is the bull [S5][S6]. An's consort is Antu (Sumerian; 'Anatum' in some accounts) [S5]. An is the father of Enlil (the air/storm god) and, in some accounts, Enki (the freshwater god) [S5]. The 'An' is also a title: the 'An' is the divine, the 'godhead' itself [S5].
interesting_facts: The sky god, the supreme deity of the Sumerian pantheon [S5].
'An' means 'sky/heaven' — the god is the sky itself [S5].
His symbol is the star; his animal is the bull [S5][S6].
Father of Enlil (and, in some accounts, Enki) [S5].
uncertainty_notes: An's supremacy 'declines' over time: Sumerian (supreme) → Akkadian (Enlil rises) → Babylonian (Marduk rises). This is a political/theological development, not a mythic event [S1][S6].
Audit 2026-10: entity id "mes-apas" is a legacy label (the god is An/Anu); id kept for URL stability.

name: Ki (the earth)

primary_sources.name: etcl.mca.edu — Electronic Text Corpus of cuneiform (transliterations + translations)

description_short: The earth goddess, the consort of An (the sky); the 'mother' of the world. In Sumerian cosmology, An (heaven) and Ki (earth) are the first pair.
description_long: 'Ki' is the earth goddess, the consort of An (the sky) [S5]. In Sumerian cosmology, An (heaven) and Ki (earth) are the first pair — the 'parents' of the world [S5]. Ki is the 'mother' of the world, the ground, the earth [S5]. The name 'Ki' is also the root of 'Kish' (a city) and of the 'ki' in 'kigurra' (a ritual object) [S5]. Ki is less well-attested as a deity than An: she is the earth-principle, the 'mother' of the world [S5].
interesting_facts: The earth goddess, the consort of An [S5].
The 'mother' of the world in Sumerian cosmology [S5].
uncertainty_notes: Ki is less well-attested as a distinct deity than An; she is the earth-principle [S5].
Audit 2026-10: An+Ki are parents of Enlil in the Sumerian tradition; for Enki the mother is more often Nammu. Ki's motherhood of Enki kept only where the dataset already asserted it — see Enki entry.

name: Apsu (the primeval freshwater)
domains: the sweet water beneath the earth

description_short: The primeval freshwater, the 'deep' beneath the earth; in the Atrahasis and Enuma Elish, Apsu is the god of the fresh water who is slain (in Atrahasis) or overthrown (in Enuma Elish).
description_long: 'Apsu' (also 'Abzu') is the primeval freshwater, the 'deep' beneath the earth — the sweet water that underlies the world [S3][S5]. In Sumerian cosmology, Apsu (the fresh water) and Tiamat (the salt water) are the two primeval waters [S3][S5]. In the Atrahasis, Apsu (the god of the fresh water) is slain by Enki (and the gods) because his noise (the noise of humanity) disturbs his rest [S3]. In the Enuma Elish, Apsu's role is taken by Apsu (the fresh water) who is slain by Ea (Enki's Akkadian name) [S1]. Apsu is the 'deep', the primeval fresh water, the source of life [S3][S5].
interesting_facts: The primeval freshwater, the 'deep' beneath the earth [S3][S5].
Slain in the Atrahasis (by Enki) and the Enuma Elish (by Ea) [S1][S3].
One of the two primeval waters (with Tiamat) [S3][S5].
uncertainty_notes: Apsu's 'slaying' in the Atrahasis is the creation-of-humanity story: humanity is made from Apsu's flesh/blood to relieve the gods of their labor [S3].

name: Tiamat

primary_sources.name: Enuma Elish (Babylonian Creation Epic)
primary_sources.date: Old Babylonian version c. 18th c. BCE; standard form c. 1100-1000 BCE

description_short: The primeval saltwater, the 'salt sea', the embodiment of chaos; in the Enuma Elish she is the great adversary of Marduk, whose slain body is used to create the world.
description_long: 'Tiamat' is the primeval saltwater, the 'salt sea', the embodiment of the primordial state [S1][S5]. In Sumerian cosmology, Tiamat (the salt water) and Apsu (the fresh water) are the two primeval waters [S3][S5]. In the Enuma Elish, Tiamat is the great adversary of Marduk: she raises an army of monsters (led by Kingu) to fight Marduk, and is slain by Marduk, who splits her body in two to make the sky (the upper half) and the earth (the lower half) [S1]. Tiamat is the embodiment of chaos, the 'salt sea', the primordial state from which the ordered world emerges [S1][S5].
interesting_facts: The primeval saltwater, the embodiment of chaos [S1][S5].
The great adversary of Marduk in the Enuma Elish [S1].

uncertainty_notes: Tiamat's 'chaos' role is a later (Babylonian) interpretation; in earlier (Sumerian) texts she is simply the salt-water principle [S5].

description_short: The general of Tiamat's army in the Enuma Elish; he holds the 'Tablet of Destinies' (the symbol of cosmic authority); he is slain by Marduk.
description_long: Kingu is the general of Tiamat's army in the Enuma Elish [S1]. He holds the 'Tablet of Destinies' (the 'me' of kingship, the symbol of cosmic authority) on Tiamat's behalf [S1]. Marduk slays Kingu and takes the Tablet of Destinies; from Kingu's blood, Marduk creates humanity (in the Enuma Elish) [S1]. Kingu is the 'crown' (his title: he holds the 'Tablet of Destinies') [S1].

name: Enlil
sacred_objects: the horned crown (the symbol of kingship)

primary_sources.name: Enuma Elish (Babylonian Creation Epic)

description_short: The 'air/wind/storm' god, the 'breath' of the world; in the Akkadian and Babylonian periods he is the king of the gods. His great temple was at Nippur. He is the 'decider' — he makes the fates (the 'me').
description_long: 'Enlil' (Akkadian 'Ellil') is the 'air/wind/storm' god, the 'breath' of the world — his name means 'the breath of Enlil' (the wind that gives life) [S5][S6]. In the Sumerian period, Enlil was one of the great gods; in the Akkadian and Babylonian periods, he became the king of the gods (the 'Anum' — the supreme deity) [S1][S6]. Enlil's great temple was at Nippur (the 'Ekur' — the 'mountain house') [S5][S6]. Enlil is the 'decider': he makes the fates (the 'me' — the divine decrees that order the world) [S5]. Enlil's consort is Ninlil [S5]. Enlil's children include Nanna (the moon god), Ninhursag (the earth-mother, in some accounts), and Nergal (the underworld god, in some accounts) [S5]. Enlil is the god who decrees the flood (in the Atrahasis and the Gilgamesh flood-story) [S2][S3].
interesting_facts: The 'air/wind/storm' god, the 'breath' of the world [S5].
King of the gods in the Akkadian/Babylonian period [S1][S6].
His great temple was at Nippur (the 'Ekur') [S5][S6].
The 'decider' — he makes the fates (the 'me') [S5].
Decrees the flood (Atrahasis, Gilgamesh) [S2][S3].
uncertainty_notes: Enlil's 'supremacy' is period-specific: Sumerian (one of the great gods) → Akkadian/Babylonian (king of the gods) → Late Babylonian (Marduk rises) [S1][S6].

name: Enki (Ea)
symbols: the goat-fish (the 'adapa' fish, in some accounts)

primary_sources.name: Enuma Elish (Babylonian Creation Epic)

description_short: The freshwater god of wisdom, magic, and the 'me' (the divine decrees); his great temple was at Eridu (the oldest city in Sumerian tradition). In the Atrahasis and the Gilgamesh flood-story, he saves the flood-hero against Enlil's will.
description_long: 'Enki' (Sumerian; 'Ea' in Akkadian) is the freshwater god of wisdom, magic, and the 'me' (the divine decrees) [S5][S6]. His great temple was at Eridu (the 'Aabzu' — the 'house of the deep'), the oldest city in Sumerian tradition [S5][S6]. Enki is the god of wisdom, magic, and the 'me' — the divine decrees that order the world [S5]. He is the 'apku' (the sage), the patron of the scribes and the craftsmen [S5]. In the Atrahasis and the Gilgamesh flood-story, Enki (Ea) saves the flood-hero (Atrahasis/Utnapishtim) against Enlil's will, by whispering to the hero to build a boat [S2][S3]. Enki is the father of Marduk, the Babylonian king of the gods, and so ancestor of Marduk's son, the scribe-god Nabu [S5]. In the Enuma Elish, Enki (Ea) overthrows Apsu, the primeval freshwater, and his son Marduk shapes the world and humankind from the slain [S1].
interesting_facts: The freshwater god of wisdom, magic, and the 'me' [S5].
His great temple was at Eridu (the 'Aabzu') [S5][S6].
Saves the flood-hero against Enlil's will (Atrahasis, Gilgamesh) [S2][S3].
The 'apku' (the sage), patron of the scribes [S5].
uncertainty_notes: Enki's 'wisdom' role is central; his relationship to the 'me' (the divine decrees) is complex: he is both a holder and a distributor of the 'me' [S5].
Audit 2026-10: mother is Nammu (primeval sea) in Sumerian tradition (Enki's birth cycle); Nammu is not modeled as an entity. Father An per the standard genealogy.

Ninlil's myth: in one Sumerian text, Enlil seduces Ninlil (while she is in the underworld), and she bears Nanna (the moon) there [S5]. Ninlil is the 'light' of Enlil — the moonlight that follows the storm-god [S5].

name: Nanna (Sin)

description_short: The moon god, the god of time, the calendar, and fate; his great temple was at Ur. In Sumerian tradition he is the son of Enlil; in Akkadian he is called Sin. Father of Utu (Shamash) and Inanna (Ishtar).
description_long: 'Nanna' (Sumerian; 'Sin' in Akkadian) is the moon god, the god of time, the calendar, and fate [S5][S6]. His great temple was at Ur (the 'Ehursag') [S5][S6]. In Sumerian tradition, Nanna is the son of Enlil (and Ninlil) [S5]. In Akkadian, he is called Sin [S5]. Nanna is the father of Utu (the sun god, Akkadian 'Shamash') and Inanna (the love/war goddess, Akkadian 'Ishtar') [S5]. The moon-god decrees fates (the 'me') — the moon's phases are the measure of time [S5]. Nanna's 'time' role makes him the god of the calendar and of the measurement of the months [S5].

description_short: The sun god, the god of justice and the 'light' that reveals the truth; in Akkadian he is called Shamash. The sun-god travels through the underworld by night (the 'journey of the sun through the Duat' equivalent).
description_long: 'Utu' (Sumerian; 'Shamash' in Akkadian) is the sun god, the god of justice and the 'light' that reveals the truth [S5][S6]. The sun-god travels across the sky by day and through the underworld by night (the 'journey of the sun') [S5]. Utu is the god of justice: he 'sees' all, and his light reveals the truth [S5]. In the 'Utnapishtim' flood-story and other texts, Utu is a 'judge' who sees the wickedness of humanity [S2]. Utu is the brother of Inanna (Ishtar) [S5]. Utu's 'justice' role makes him the patron of the oaths and the courts [S5].

name: Inanna (Ishtar)

primary_sources.name: etcl.mca.edu — Electronic Text Corpus of cuneiform (transliterations + translations)

description_short: The great goddess of love, sexuality, war, and fertility; 'queen of heaven'; the morning/evening star (Venus); her great temple was at Uruk. In Akkadian she is Ishtar. She descends to the underworld and is restored (the 'Inanna's Descent' myth).
description_long: 'Inanna' (Sumerian; 'Ishtar' in Akkadian) is the great goddess of love, sexuality, war, and fertility [S4][S5][S6]. She is the 'queen of heaven', the morning/evening star (Venus) [S5]. Her great temple was at Uruk (the 'Eanna') [S5][S6]. Inanna is the most complex of the Mesopotamian deities: she is both the goddess of love and the goddess of war, both the life-giver and the death-bringer [S4][S5]. The great myth of 'Inanna's Descent to the Underworld': Inanna descends to the underworld to attend the funeral of her sister Ereshkigal (the underworld-goddess), is stripped of her powers at the seven gates, is killed, and is restored by Enki (who sends a being to bring her back) [S4][S5]. The 'Descent' is a myth of death and resurrection, and is one of the oldest attested 'descent-and-return' myths [S4][S5]. Inanna's 'Venus' role (the morning/evening star) makes her the goddess of the 'star' (the eight-pointed star is her symbol) [S5].
interesting_facts: The great goddess of love, sexuality, war, and fertility [S4][S5].
The 'queen of heaven', the morning/evening star (Venus) [S5].
Her great temple was at Uruk (the 'Eanna') [S5][S6].
The 'Inanna's Descent' myth (death and resurrection) [S4][S5].
The eight-pointed star is her symbol [S5].
uncertainty_notes: Inanna's 'love' and 'war' roles are not separate: she is a single, complex goddess who embodies both [S4][S5].
The 'Descent' myth has multiple versions (Sumerian c. 1900-1700 BCE; later Akkadian versions); the details vary [S4].

description_short: The queen of the underworld, the 'dark' goddess of the dead; Inanna's sister (in some accounts) or adversary. In the 'Descent' myth, Inanna attends her funeral (or is her guest) and is killed there.
description_long: 'Ereshkigal' is the queen of the underworld, the 'dark' goddess of the dead [S4][S5]. She is the lord of the 'irigal' (the underworld) [S5]. In 'Inanna's Descent,' Inanna travels down to the underworld and is judged by Ereshkigal and the Anunnaki, struck down and hung on a hook before her restoration [S4][S5]. Ereshkigal is Inanna's sister (in some accounts) or her adversary [S4][S5]. Ereshkigal's consort is Nergal (the underworld-god, in some accounts) [S5]. Ereshkigal is the 'dark' counterpart of Inanna (the 'light' goddess) [S4][S5].

name: Nergal

primary_sources.name: etcl.mca.edu — Electronic Text Corpus of cuneiform (transliterations + translations)

description_short: The underworld god, the 'lord of the netherworld', the god of the plague; in some accounts he is Ereshkigal's consort. In the 'Nergal and Ereshkigal' myth, he 'rapes' (or marries) Ereshkigal and becomes her consort.
description_long: 'Nergal' is the underworld god, the 'lord of the netherworld', the god of the plague [S5]. In some accounts, he is Ereshkigal's consort [S5]. The 'Nergal and Ereshkigal' myth: Nergal 'rapes' (or marries) Ereshkigal, and becomes her consort and the lord of the underworld [S5]. Nergal is the god of the plague and the 'dark' power of the underworld [S5]. He is also a war-god (in some accounts) [S5]. Nergal's 'plague' role makes him a feared deity — his 'dark' power is the power of death and disease [S5].

Audit 2026-10: Erra/Nergal is "seed of Enlil, offspring of Ninlil" (Erra Epic I); as Ereshkigal's consort he is the "Nergal and Ereshkigal" myth. A duplicate entity for him was merged into this one (audit F35).

name: Marduk

primary_sources.name: Enuma Elish (Babylonian Creation Epic)
primary_sources.date: Old Babylonian version c. 18th c. BCE; standard form c. 1100-1000 BCE

description_short: The Babylonian supreme god, the 'storm' god, the king of the gods in the Babylonian period; in the Enuma Elish he slays Tiamat and creates the world from her body. His great temple was at Babylon (the Esagila).
description_long: 'Marduk' is the Babylonian supreme god, the 'storm' god, the king of the gods in the Babylonian period [S1][S6]. In the Enuma Elish, Marduk is chosen by the gods to fight Tiamat; he slays her with his bow, net, and 'rakasu' winds, and splits her body in two to make the sky (the upper half) and the earth (the lower half) [S1]. From Kingu's blood (Tiamat's general), Marduk creates humanity [S1]. Marduk takes the 'Tablet of Destinies' (the symbol of cosmic authority) from Kingu [S1]. Marduk's great temple was at Babylon (the Esagila) [S6]. Marduk's 'supremacy' is a political/theological development: as Babylon rose to power (Old Babylonian period, c. 2000-1600 BCE), Marduk rose to be the king of the gods [S1][S6]. The Enuma Elish (the 'New Year' festival text) is the great myth of Marduk's supremacy [S1].

In the Enuma Elish, he slays Tiamat and creates the world [S1].
Takes the 'Tablet of Destinies' from Kingu [S1].

uncertainty_notes: Marduk's 'supremacy' is period-specific: Old Babylonian (rises) → Neo-Babylonian (supreme) → Achaemenid/Persian (declines) [S1][S6].
Audit 2026-10: Enuma Elish I 36-39 — Marduk is son of Ea (Enki) and Damkina, grandson of An and Tiamat (the "Tiamat" here is Ea's salt-water grandmother layer); Damkina not modeled as an entity.

name: Ningal

primary_sources.name: etcl.mca.edu — Electronic Text Corpus of cuneiform (transliterations + translations)

description_short: Ningal, wife of the moon-god Nanna and mother of Utu (the sun) and Inanna (the morning star) — the moon's bright consort at Ur.
description_long: Ningal is the consort of Nanna, the moon god, and the mother of Utu (Shamash), the sun, and Inanna (Ishtar), the morning star [S5]. Her name means 'Great Lady,' and she shared the great temple of Ur with Nanna, invoked alongside him in the city's hymns and laments [S5]. Ningal is less fully developed than her children in the surviving texts, but her cult at Ur was long-lived [S5].

name: Nabu

primary_sources.name: etcl.mca.edu — Electronic Text Corpus of cuneiform (transliterations + translations)

description_short: God of writing, wisdom, and the scribal arts; son of Marduk, and heir to the written authority of Babylon's king of the gods.
description_long: 'Nabu' is the god of writing, wisdom, and the scribal arts, the patron of the scribes [S5]. He is the son of Marduk, the Babylonian king of the gods, and serves as his vizier, holding the written authority of the Tablet of Destinies [S5]. His great temple, the Ezida, stood at Borsippa, and his art of writing served the ordering of the world and the recording of fate [S5].
interesting_facts: The god of writing and wisdom [S5].
Son of Enki (Ea) [S5].
The patron of the scribes [S5].
uncertainty_notes: Audit 2026-10: mother given as Nisaba (or Tasmetu as consort) in different lists; neither modeled. Father: Marduk (standard first-millennium genealogy).
